title: The definite article

objectives.can: Give the case, number and gender of any form of the article.
Recognise ten of the commonest nouns of the New Testament.

explanation.summary: Greek has one article, ὁ ἡ τό, 'the'. It is the commonest word in the New Testament, and because it changes its form to match its noun, it is the quickest way to learn what case, number and gender are.

sections.heading: One word, many forms
body: English 'the' never changes. The Greek article has a different form for each gender (masculine, feminine, neuter), each number (singular, plural) and each case (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative). The article always agrees with its noun in all three: in ὁ λόγος both words are nominative singular masculine; in τὸν θεόν both are accusative singular masculine.
So the article tells you about its noun. If you can read the article, you already know the case, number and gender of the word it belongs to, even when the noun's own ending is unfamiliar.

sections.heading: What the cases are for
body: A case shows what a word is doing in its clause. The nominative names the subject; the genitive often means 'of'; the dative often means 'to', 'for', 'in' or 'with'; the accusative names the object. These are first approximations: each case has its own lesson.
Because the endings carry this information, Greek word order is free to do other work, such as emphasis.

sections.heading: How to recognise the forms
body: The masculine and feminine nominatives (ὁ, ἡ, οἱ, αἱ) begin with a rough breathing and have no accent of their own. Every other form begins with τ.
The genitive and dative forms carry a circumflex (τοῦ, τῆς, τῷ, τῇ, τῶν, τοῖς, ταῖς). The dative singular always has an iota subscript. The genitive plural is τῶν in all three genders.
The neuter nominative and accusative are always alike: τό in the singular, τά in the plural.

sections.heading: No word for 'a'
body: Greek has no indefinite article. A noun without the article may be translated with 'a' or with nothing, and is sometimes definite all the same: names, abstract nouns and nouns after prepositions often go without the article. The presence or absence of the article is a matter of Greek idiom and has to be read in context.

misunderstandings: The article ἡ (feminine nominative) must not be confused with ἤ ('or') or ἦν ('was'): the article has a rough breathing and no accent.
ὁ (the article) is not ὅ (a relative pronoun, 'which'), which carries an accent.
A noun without the article is not automatically indefinite. In John 1:1 θεός stands without the article as the predicate of the sentence.

deeper.heading: Where the article came from
body: In Homer ὁ ἡ τό is still a demonstrative pronoun, 'this one, that one'. Traces remain in later Greek: ὁ δέ at the start of a sentence means 'and he', and ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ means 'the one … the other'. You will meet both in the Gospels.

examples.analysis: ὁ is nominative singular masculine, agreeing with λόγος, the subject: 'the Word'. τὸν is accusative singular masculine, agreeing with θεόν after the preposition πρός: 'with God'. Greek uses the article with θεόν here where English does not.
